content.text: very good, can we have the grade of a cell (color) reflect a combination of its balance and circularity? and then the probability of selecting the next cell is propotional to the badness of its score

items.text:
Yes. Using our current normalization, define cell \(i\)’s **badness**
\[
B_i=(1-C_i)+\frac{G_i}{59.86},
\]
where \(G_i\) is its modeled mean neighbor-weight gap. Lower is better.

- **Color:** shade cells by \(B_i\), with worse cells darker.
- **Selection:** choose the next cell with probability
  \[
  p_i=\frac{B_i}{\sum_j B_j}.
  \]
  If all scores are zero, choose uniformly.

Keep the 50/50 choice of movement direction and the existing acceptance rule.

**This changes scheduling:** if we sample afresh after each turn, a cell can be selected several times while another receives no turn. We would call 100 selections a *batch*, rather than a round visiting every cell once.

Alternatively, weighted sampling **without replacement** preserves one turn per cell per round, while giving worse cells earlier turns. Which do you want?

items.text:
**Yes. Every cell gets exactly one turn in every complete round.**

The turns happen sequentially, not simultaneously. After a cell’s turn, its neighbors can move and change its polygon. That cell waits until the next round to respond.

Round 58 was interrupted after 60 turns, so it was **not a complete round**.

Yes—**every cell gets exactly one turn per complete round**, in random order. A turn can end without movement if the proposal fails.

We stopped **partway through round 58**, after 60 of 100 turns. The cell labeled 62 had already moved on turn 14. Its neighbors then moved and changed its shape, but it would only get another turn in round 59.
